Let me just quickly comment on the paper by Hong Wang et al. because this has a very common feature in that the theorem statement is very unclear and any naive formalization will be most likely incorrect. The issue is that they write "any function" (they don't even specify the codomain, but most like it is C and I am sure it could be generalized to any Banach space unless something really funny is happening). In mathlib that would be a bare function, but then you run into the obvious problem that the Fourier transform has a junk value 0 if f is not integrable. So you would probably be led to assume L1, but then you need to estimate the L4 norm (do you do eLpNorm? again problems with junk values? etc). Later on you see them using Plancherel, so maybe you also need to assume that f is in L2. So what is actually going on here? My best guess is that you prove the estimate for docs#SchwartzMap and then use density (unclear what the right space is, but it will certainly be contained in L4, so docs#SchwartzMap.denseRange_toLpCLM works). Btw the word Schwartz is not mentioned in the paper, because everyone in the field knows that this is what you do. There is a subtle point, that I can't answer unless reading the paper in full, which is whether the finiteness of the RHS implies that f is in L4, i.e., is the estimate claimed to be a regularity-improving estimate or do you have to assume the LHS to be finite a-priori. This can be very important (especially for the applications such as their Theorem 1.2), but here it is unclear.
The point I want to make is just that without any proper knowledge of the field it is very easy to formalize something that is either obviously wrong or not really what is claimed.
I'm glad you appreciate how much fun we've been having with this project :-) In fact it really opened my eyes to see the difference between what we tell people we do, and what we actually do.
Sometimes we had to email the authors with questions like "is X supposed to be measurable because if it isn't what does what you're saying even mean?"

The fun thing here is that you could also take an arbitrary compactly supported distribution (because they assume that the FT of f is compactly supported) and then its inverse Fourier transform is a function. But then the RHS doesn't make sense, but you could additionally assume that the distribution is represented by a functions that can be written as on the RHS.
I don't think this is the case here, but what I want to say is: it could be that part of the statement is that the function is measurable, so that the FT is not distributional, but the usual one.

Just to add another point to Moritz, I think when they say the support of the fourier transform of f lies in some region what they really mean is that you regard f∈L4f \in L^4f∈L4 as a distribution, then you take the fourier transform of the distribution and use Distribution.dsupport.

I guess this can be pretty confusing and this is especially common in harmonic analysis/PDEs... People abuse the language that "an operator is bounded from Lp to Lq" but it is often the case that this operator is only well defined on a dense subspace (that consists of some nice functions) of Lp and what they really mean is that "this (p,q)-estimate holds on the dense subspace so this operator admits an extension to Lp"

Is the project open to external contributions? I would be interested to submit some PDE problem statements.

If you want some PDE project, then either open a new thread or dm me what kind of result you would be interested in getting in and then we figure out what is missing and would be feasible.

Moritz Doll said:

This can be very important (especially for the applications such as their Theorem 1.2)

Is this really important for Theorem 1.2? I would expect that a density argument for solutions to the wave equation should easily work here.

Moritz Doll said:

and I am sure it could be generalized to any Banach space

I would not be so sure. A lot of harmonic analysis fails for general Banach spaces (for example, Bourgain showed that the Hilbert transform is only bounded when the Banach space has UMD).

Joris van Winden said:

Moritz Doll said:

This can be very important (especially for the applications such as their Theorem 1.2)

Is this really important for Theorem 1.2? I would expect that a density argument for solutions to the wave equation should easily work here.

Probably in this case it should be fine, but there are certainly examples where you have to be careful.

Maybe I shouldn't have written any, the better claim is that there should be obvious generalizations for certain parts of the argument that might be helpful in other contexts and the experts know exactly which parts generalize and which parts don't. My point was mainly there is a lot of ambiguity here.

If possible, I think a new thread is preferable. I feel like a lot more work in analysis has been going on behind closed doors as opposed to other topics, and that is probably suboptimal
What happens if you ask an AI to explain the theorem statement formally I wonder? Do they see all these subtleties yet?

I might be somewhat guilty of that. Every now and then I tried to get other people interested, but the results have not been any good. So now I mainly work on things myself, and PR them to mathlib if I feel like it (we could have had Sobolev spaces in 2023 or so, but I got too annoyed and also my job was to prove theorems about the Klein-Gordon equation).
The fact that most people just want to throw a bot farm at any formalization problem doesn't help either for open discussions.

We didn't use any AI when making the formalisations but we did use AI to check and it was quite good at spotting things like this. For example we had a function in one paper which the authors assumed was nonzero in a theorem statement so we dutifully assumed f \ne 0 and then a bot took one look at the paper and the formalisation and said "well in the proof "nonzero" is taken to mean "nonzero in L^2" so what you have formalised doesn't reflect what they mean" :-/
